The search tool hit its limit before I could reach the Lutheran, Orthodox, Pentecostal (ag.org) or Baptist sites (desiringgod, gty, spurgeon), or bibleodyssey.org. Several pages I could only read as long excerpts in the search results, not in full. Everything below comes from what I actually read. There are no notes for v. 2's wider debates, v. 10 or v. 14's debates because I found nothing on them.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- "Finally" doesn't mean Paul is wrapping up. It literally means "for the rest" and starts the closing, practical part of the letter. "Ask" is a calm, friendly request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- "What you received from us" suggests the apostles taught new believers a set moral code, almost like a well-known handbook on how to live. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- Paul was glad they were growing but still wanted them to grow "more and more." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Matthew Henry: holding on to the faith isn't enough. Believers should keep growing in good works, and talking well without living well gets no one to heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_004.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: Paul taught them how to *walk*, not how to talk. Daily life was to be led by the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 2**
- "By the authority of the Lord Jesus" means Christ inspired Paul to give these commands. It doesn't mean Christ delivered them in person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- Henry: the apostles passed on what Christ commanded rather than making up rules of their own. Church leaders today shouldn't "lord it over" believers either. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_004.cfm

**v. 3**
- Being made holy ("sanctification") means being set apart from a godless culture and its sexual immorality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Ellicott: God's aim isn't only to convert or save us. He wants us holy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- Pulpit: "God's will" here means what God desires and delights in, which people can resist. It isn't his fixed decree. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html
- Precept Austin: in Thessalonica's culture, sex outside marriage was even treated as an act of worship. No appeal to Christian freedom can justify it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_43-5

**v. 4** (does "his vessel" mean his body or his wife?)
- Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that some read "vessel" as "wife," as though Paul were urging marriage. He thinks Paul more likely means each person's own body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Ellicott says the body. The verb means "gain control of," as in rescuing the body from misuse and using it rightly. He argues against "wife" for three reasons: it would forbid staying single, it doesn't fit "know how to," and the Greek wording doesn't support it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/4-4.htm
- Several older commentators read it as "wife." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes it as "acquire his own wife" to avoid immorality, pointing to 1 Pet 3:7 and Jewish usage. Matthew Poole mentions the wife view. Gill says it could be either, because Jewish writers used the word for both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/4-4.htm
- Adam Clarke leans toward "wife." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/4-4.html
- Precept Austin lists ancient and modern names on each side. For "body": Theodoret, Calvin and others. For "wife": Theodore of Mopsuestia, Frame and others. It also points out that in 1 Pet 3:7 both husband and wife count as "vessels." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_44-5

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the word for "lust" describes something that happens *to* a person, a helpless passivity. Giving in to it means losing control of yourself, not mastering yourself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- People who don't know God lack the spiritual resources for purity. Christians have them, so they should live differently. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Henry: it's shameful for reason and conscience to be ruled by bodily appetites. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_004.cfm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: chastity is also a matter of fairness to your brother. "In this matter" is a tactful way of referring to sexual sin. The Lord's vengeance means Judgment Day, not just natural consequences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- Guzik gives four reasons for sexual purity in vv. 6–8. The first is that God punishes this sin even when no one else finds out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Precept Austin: just as stealing wrongs a neighbour, sexual immorality wrongs other people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_46-8
- Henry mentions that some read v. 6 as a wider warning against cheating people in business. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_004.cfm

**v. 7**
- Impurity isn't part of the terms on which God called us. The verse sums up the passage by returning to v. 3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/4.htm
- "Not" comes first in the Greek for emphasis: God absolutely did not call us to impurity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_46-8

**v. 8**
- Rejecting this command means rejecting God, not just a human teacher. Guzik thinks Paul was trying to prevent sin here, not rebuking a sin already happening. The gift of the Spirit gives believers the power to overcome. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Pulpit: what's being rejected could be the commands, the call to holiness, or Paul himself as God's messenger. Several commentators add that impurity is an insult to the Holy Spirit who lives in the believer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/4-8.htm

**v. 9**
- The Thessalonians were "taught by God" about love, yet everyone still needs reminding. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Henry: the Spirit teaches better than any human teacher. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_004.cfm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the Greek means "make it your ambition to be quiet." Their ambition had been to stir things up. Pulpit puts it as "be ambitious not to be ambitious." Poole and Gill tie the verse to idle busybodies (2 Thess 3:11). Gill also infers that most church members were poor manual workers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/4-11.htm
- Pulpit: Jesus and Paul both worked with their hands, and Christians should be too busy with their own work to judge their neighbours. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik ties "lack nothing" back to 3:10: following Paul's teaching leads to maturity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Pulpit: Christians can't expect fair treatment from outsiders unless they deal honestly with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 13**
- The Thessalonians worried that believers who died before Christ returned would miss out on his coming. Guzik compares Christian grief to seeing someone off on a long trip. He also quotes Hiebert: "sleep" doesn't mean the soul is unconscious. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Barnes describes pagan funeral customs: hired mourners, beating the breast, tearing hair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/4-13.htm
- Pulpit: "no hope" means no hope of life after death or of resurrection. Christianity doesn't call for cold indifference to grief. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik quotes Morris: Jesus will bring the believing dead with him, so they won't miss his coming. Our bond with Christ is stronger than death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/

**v. 15**
- Guzik quotes Thomas: "we who are alive" sets an example of eager expectation for the church in every age. It wasn't a mistaken promise that Christ would come in Paul's lifetime. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/
- Pulpit notes that some argue Paul expected to be alive at the Lord's coming, and says the point is still being debated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html
- Precept Austin thinks the "we" shows Paul fully expected to meet the Lord himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59702/

**v. 16**
- The point is that the believing dead won't be left out. They rise first. Until then, they aren't in "soul sleep." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/

**v. 17**
- The rapture-related views are in Section 2.
- Constable: living believers are changed and the dead are raised, and both meet Christ ("apantesis," as in Matt 25:6 and Acts 28:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/4-17.html
- Coffman: believers don't stay "in the air." They go with Christ to the new heavens and new earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/4-17.html
- Barnes guessed that the judgment might take place in the air. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/4-17.html
- Precept Austin: "together" means the living and the raised dead are caught up at the same moment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_417-18
- Pulpit: Christ's coming isn't a passing visit. It ends in Christians living with him for good. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 18**
- We comfort one another by remembering Christ's return and our eternal union with him, especially when believing loved ones die. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-4/

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 3, Methodist/Wesleyan:** John Wesley defines sanctification as "entire holiness of heart and life." This is the Wesleyan emphasis on full holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 4:** Wesley reads "vessel" as "wife." Marriage is meant to overcome natural desires, not inflame them. Calvin is listed with the "body" reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-thessalonians-4.html and https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_44-5

**v. 6:** Wesley reads it as adultery, "violating his bed." He counts three things forbidden in vv. 3–6: sex outside marriage, uncontrolled passion within marriage, and breaking the marriage covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-thessalonians-4.html

**v. 15:** Wesley says Paul speaks as part of one body of believers across all ages. He wasn't claiming the Lord's day was close at hand. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-thessalonians-4.html

**vv. 16–17, timing of the "rapture":**
- **Pre-tribulation view** (GotQuestions, bible.org): the rapture can happen at any moment and is separate from the Second Coming. At the rapture Christ comes *for* his saints in the air; later he comes *with* them to earth. Both sites say the church won't be on earth during the tribulation. https://www.gotquestions.org/meet-the-Lord-in-the-air.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/7-rapture
- GotQuestions also notes that whether the rapture and the Second Coming are two events is much debated. https://www.gotquestions.org/rapture-of-the-church.html
- **One coming, after the tribulation** (The Gospel Coalition essay): the passage is about the resurrection of believers and says nothing about the church being removed before the tribulation. "Coming" (parousia) means Christ's visible return, as it does everywhere else in Thessalonians. The passage draws on Jesus' teaching in the Olivet Discourse (Matt 24). "Meet" suggests believers come back to earth with Jesus. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-rapture-question/
- **Baptist (second-hand):** Catholic Answers quotes Baptist theologian Dale Moody, who called the pre-tribulation rapture "biblically bankrupt." https://www.catholic.com/tract/the-rapture
- **Methodist:** Wesley says the wicked stay below while the righteous are cleared and sit with their Lord at the judgment. "With the Lord" means in heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-thessalonians-4.html
- **Pentecostal and Lutheran:** I couldn't reach these. Guzik's page has some timing discussion, but I only saw a cut-off excerpt.

## 3. Other views

**v. 4, modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** "Vessel" most likely means "body," and "wife" is less likely. The notes mention J. Smith (2000), who argues it is probably a polite term for the sexual organs. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=1Th+4%3A3%2C4

**v. 17, "meet":**
- The Greek word was used for a group going out to welcome an important visitor and escort him back. https://biblehub.com/q/1_Thess_4_17_s_link_to_rapture_concept.htm
- "Rapture" comes from the Latin translation of "caught up" (*rapiemur*). https://www.gotquestions.org/meet-the-Lord-in-the-air.html

**vv. 15–17, Catholic:**
- There is one glorious coming at the end of time, with the general resurrection and judgment. A secret, early removal is rejected as a 19th-century idea (Darby, Scofield). https://www.catholic.com/tract/end-of-the-world-catholic-view-on-the-rapture
- The trumpet and the resurrection of the dead point to the end of time. 2 Thess 2 places the Antichrist before "our gathering to him." Believers go up to escort the coming King, as ancient cities did for dignitaries. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/answering-the-rapture-challenge
- Jimmy Akin: Catholics accept the event in v. 17 itself, just not the extra pre-tribulation framework. https://www.catholic.com/video/can-catholics-believe-in-the-rapture

**Orthodox, and popular teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** not found.
